medical.title: Imaging technique reveals the metabolic states of individual immune cells
medical.summary: When a patient is facing certain cancers or an immune condition, clinicians turn to white blood cells for clues about the progression of both diseases and their treatments. From a standard blood draw, a clinical lab isolates peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), which are predominantly immune cells, and then counts the abundance of different cell types, along with some basic measures of how they're functioning.

medical.title: Protein buildup may shape cancer drug response
medical.summary: The way cancer-causing proteins accumulate in tumors may influence how effectively a promising new generation of medicines can remove them, a study suggests. Researchers found that PROTAC (Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras) drugs were more effective at removing proteins that build up because they are not broken down properly than proteins that cancer cells continually produce in large amounts.

medical.title: Four-country study brings digital health coaching into everyday maternity care
medical.summary: Researchers at University College Dublin (UCD) have published the full study protocol for Bump2Baby & Me+ (B2B&Me+) in the journal PLOS One. The study tests how a digital health coaching program for pregnant women at risk of gestational diabetes performs when it moves out of a clinical trial and into routine hospital care. The publication coincides with the close of the study's recruitment phase, which began in December 2025 across hospitals in Ireland, Spain, Poland and Norway.

medical.title: Low-dose THC keeps breast cancer cells in tumor models from reverting to an aggressive state
medical.summary: Recent discoveries have revealed that breast cancer cells are more flexible than previously thought. Some can change from a differentiated state, when a mature cell has taken on a specific function, back to a more stem-like state. From there, they can become more invasive and resistant to treatment.

medical.title: Stress and depression, not heart damage, may drive long-term breast cancer fatigue
medical.summary: For breast cancer survivors, new research shows that feelings of depression and perceptions of psychological stress make the biggest difference in whether they experience fatigue up to two years after chemotherapy started.

medical.title: Children with speech sound disorders often face additional challenges
medical.summary: Speech sound disorders (SSD) in children are a common group of developmental difficulties that affect how speech sounds are planned and produced. In her thesis, "Oral Motor, Sensory and Developmental Indicators in Children with Speech Sound Disorders: A Clinical Cohort Study," Helena Björelius studied children ages 4 to 9 who had been referred for specialist assessment of speech and oral motor difficulties. The aim was to increase understanding of factors beyond speech itself, including chewing efficiency, sensory processing and medical and developmental risk factors.

medical.title: Severe asthma remains active in most despite widespread biologic treatment
medical.summary: Severe asthma affects around 5%–10% of all people with asthma and can involve recurrent exacerbations, impaired lung function and the need for corticosteroid treatment. In recent years, biologic therapies have improved treatment options for many patients.

medical.title: Investment in blood cancer research has saved nearly 26 million years of life, but disparities remain
medical.summary: Over the past 75 years, advances in the treatment of major blood cancers have saved more than 25 million years of life in the United States, according to results of an analysis led by researchers at Blood Cancer United and published in Blood Advances. But the gains have not reached everyone equally: survival progress remains limited for people diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and for Black individuals across most major blood cancer types.

medical.title: Three distinct BMI trajectories identified in people with type 2 diabetes
medical.summary: A study by the University of Eastern Finland identified three distinct body mass index (BMI) trajectories among people with type 2 diabetes. Over the 10-year follow-up period, the BMI trajectories were associated with significant differences in comorbidities, diabetes medication and health care service use.

medical.title: Major study reveals key differences in bowel cancer before and after age 50
medical.summary: One of Australia's largest real-world studies of younger adults with advanced bowel cancer has identified important differences between cancers diagnosed before and after age 50, which could help doctors tailor treatments for younger adults more effectively.

medical.title: Supplement plus chemotherapy boosts pancreatic cancer survival
medical.summary: When added to standard chemotherapy, a clinical version of the dietary supplement L-glutamine improved survival in an early-phase trial of patients with advanced pancreatic cancer. The study, led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University investigators, was published in Nature Cancer.

medical.title: Men with low or high testosterone may have a higher risk of irregular heartbeat, review indicates
medical.summary: Men with either low or high testosterone levels may face a higher risk of atrial fibrillation, highlighting the need for personalized testosterone treatment, according to a review of existing evidence on testosterone and heart health published in the Journal of the Endocrine Society.

medical.title: How breakfast primes the response to the hormones that manage blood sugar
medical.summary: Vanderbilt researchers have discovered why the adage, "breakfast is the most important meal of the day," holds weight—especially for the 1 in 9 adults worldwide living with diabetes. Glucose (the simplest form of sugar) is the body's main source of energy. When everything is working properly, the body regulates glucose—keeping it from spiking or crashing—and stores it until we need it.

medical.title: Mindfulness may lower blood pressure in just 8 weeks
medical.summary: Mindfulness, gratitude, and optimism training may improve blood pressure, inflammation, and other heart-health measures within just eight to 12 weeks. The strongest programs paired daily practice with regular reinforcement, suggesting that improving psychological well-being could become another tool for protecting cardiovascular health.

medical.title: London’s Ulez linked to healthier lung growth in children
medical.summary: Seven years after London introduced its Ultra Low Emission Zone, researchers are measuring the impact on children's health The post London’s Ulez linked to healthier lung growth in children appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Three discoveries that transformed how we understand nutrition
medical.summary: When we think about nutrition, we almost always picture the same key players: the mouth, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas and perhaps the gut microbiota. However, the human body is not made up of isolated compartments.

medical.title: Reaching 90 without dementia doesn’t mean you’re in the clear
medical.summary: A study of people over 90 found that dementia risk remains strongly shaped by sex, race and genetics, with women and black participants facing notably higher risks. Intriguingly, some people stayed cognitively healthy despite carrying major risk factors, potentially offering clues to how the brain can resist dementia deep into old age.

medical.title: The ethical use of AI in medical practice
medical.summary: A new ethics paper from the American College of Physicians (ACP) says that while the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical practice can improve health care efficiency and quality, it must be grounded in clinical integrity and professionalism. The paper, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, outlines three guideposts for the ethical use of AI in medical practice: rationality, self-governance and competence.

medical.title: GLP-1 RAs produce significant weight loss in adults without diabetes, with newer treatments showing greater results
medical.summary: An updated systematic review evaluating the efficacy and safety of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and coagonists among adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes found that, among currently available treatments, tirzepatide produced the greatest weight loss, while newer experimental drugs showed even larger effects.

medical.title: What to know about dementia—and ways to prevent it
medical.summary: Dementia touches many lives—in many different ways. Most people have some firsthand experience of it, whether with an aging family member, friend or neighbor. More than 6 million people in the U.S. have some type of dementia, and that number is expected to increase in the coming years as the population gets older.

medical.title: The protein gap: Researchers highlight the importance of protein during menopause
medical.summary: New analysis from CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, has identified a protein gap among women ages 40–55, with survey data showing weight gain is commonly reported by women during the typical menopausal transition.

medical.title: Stay sharp after menopause: How aerobic exercise can improve key thinking skills
medical.summary: Regular aerobic exercise—the kind that gets your heart pumping—can improve important thinking skills called executive functions, and the benefits appear especially strong for women after menopause, according to Rutgers researchers.

medical.title: Goodbye CPAP? New sleep apnea pill cuts breathing events by 44%
medical.summary: A once-nightly pill cut breathing interruptions by about 44% in a major phase 3 sleep apnea trial, while improving oxygen levels and disease severity. By strengthening the muscles that keep the airway open during sleep, AD109 could offer a new option for people unable to tolerate CPAP.

medical.title: Scientists find a human-only gene that may help explain our brainpower
medical.summary: Scientists discovered that human microglia, immune cells that help shape developing brain circuits, can take four to eight years to mature instead of just weeks as they do in mice. The unusually slow process may help explain how the human brain develops its remarkable complexity and cognitive abilities.

medical.title: High blood sugar may help cancer cells hide from the immune system
medical.summary: Researchers discovered a possible way cancer cells hide from the immune system: they build a thick, sugar-rich coating around themselves. High blood sugar can strengthen this protective shield under conditions that resemble the environment inside tumors, with the protein HSF1 playing a key role. Blocking this process could make cancer cells easier for the immune system to recognize and destroy.

science.title: Ecological collapse in the world's largest mangrove forest is a preview of what's to come
science.summary: The first thing that struck us wasn't the missing trees, but the missing water. In May 2026, we visited the Sundarbans, a mangrove forest in the delta where the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers meet in the Bay of Bengal.

science.title: Q&A: Can you trust online ratings in the age of 'review bombing'?
science.summary: Before buying a product, booking a hotel or streaming a movie, many people check online reviews. But not every glowing recommendation or one-star takedown reflects a genuine customer experience.

science.title: Resin-mounted wallaby teeth reveal rare 1,200-year-old ornaments in Queensland
science.summary: While sorting through animal bones in a rock shelter in Queensland, Australia, archaeologists came across a tooth where something was "not quite right." Stuck to the tip of its root was a blackish-brown ball of glue-like resin. Eleven more teeth with the same sticky substance were found, making them the only known instance of this type of tooth ornament found outside burials in northeastern Australia and the first in the Cape York Peninsula (CYP), the new study published in Australian Archaeology reports.

science.title: Three common study myths busted by a learning expert—and better strategies to use instead
science.summary: As high school and university students approach exam periods, study sessions often increase in frequency and intensity.

science.title: Old-growth tropical forests bear lasting legacy of ancient Maya civilization
science.summary: Rainforests in Central America that have remained largely untouched by modern human activities could bear the invisible imprint of ancient Maya civilizations. New research has found that forest structure in Belize, such as canopy height and leaf density, may be influenced by how the Maya transformed and used the land thousands of years ago.

science.title: Fieldwork safety emerges as a structural challenge for ecological research
science.summary: A new Viewpoint in the journal BioScience argues that gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV) in ecological fieldwork should be understood not as a series of isolated incidents but as a structural problem rooted in how field research is organized, with broad consequences for the knowledge such research produces.

science.title: Primary school food provision 'complex, fragmented and lacking central oversight', study reveals
science.summary: A lack of central oversight and shifting catering models in primary schools could be putting children's dietary health at risk, according to new research led by the University of York.

science.title: Some of Australia's biggest companies are planning for an unbearable climate future
science.summary: Even as unprecedented fires and heat waves rage across Europe, scientists track the retreat of Antarctic sea ice and a supercharged El Niño system heads our way, Australia's largest companies are forecasting business as usual in a much hotter world.

science.title: Growing bacteria line up single-file, then buckle in liquid crystals
science.summary: When scientists study bacteria that are not in a Petri dish or a test tube but in environments that more closely mimic their actual microbial habitats, they often find delightfully unexpected behaviors. For Sujit Datta, a professor of chemical engineering, bioengineering and biophysics at Caltech, those oddities are an invitation to apply physics to exciting new puzzles.

science.title: Drone laser scans map more than 1,000 trees across 90-acre campus
science.summary: It took one drone, 300 million laser data points and seven teams of students on foot to map Wake Forest University's trees. Led by Ovidiu Csillik, an assistant professor of remote sensing in the environment and sustainability studies program, the project produced a publicly accessible, interactive 3D digital map of more than 1,000 trees and helped the university earn international accreditation as a Level II arboretum.

science.title: Bees see the world in more ways than previously thought
science.summary: The honey bee has held a special place in vision research. It is one of the best-studied insects, and much of what scientists know about how bees perceive the world is based on studies of honey bees.

science.title: A supermassive black hole erupted in X-rays, and its radio jets followed 300 days later
science.summary: By combining roughly two decades of observations from NASA's Swift X-ray Telescope with radio monitoring, astronomers have caught a supermassive black hole at the heart of the Perseus Cluster suddenly flaring in X-rays, and about 300 days later, its powerful radio emission flared too. Their paper describing the connection between this black hole's accretion disk and the jets it launches was submitted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 13 and accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Letters.

science.title: Scientists discover why snake embryos twist into spirals
science.summary: Snake embryos begin life curled into a distinctive right-handed spiral, and scientists may finally know why. Their bodies grow faster than their guts, creating a tether that forces the lengthening embryo to buckle and twist inside the egg. Researchers reached the conclusion after studying more than 900 embryos and using CT scans to reveal the hidden anatomy behind the coils.

science.title: When exposed to air, new nanomaterial becomes magnetic at high temperatures
science.summary: While fridge magnets are great for saving favorite recipes, modern magnetic materials are useful for improving fiber optics or quantum information science technology. On most fridge magnets the atoms are arranged in a repeated lattice structure called a "spinel." These structures are made up of three types of atoms, generically referred to as atoms "A," "B" and "X."

science.title: How do you get middle schoolers to eat more fruit? Give them smoothies
science.summary: At lunchtime in rural Maine middle schools, University of Maine researchers stood at two points in the cafeteria.

science.title: Engagement-driven curation can trap culture consumers in 'overfamiliarity,' leading to less long-term satisfaction
science.summary: Sometimes you can be too good at your job. Take streaming services, like Spotify or Netflix. With engagement as their main goal, their recommendation algorithms typically identify the content a user engaged with most in the recent past and efficiently suggest more of the same. Content and genres that received limited engagement over a few weeks or months typically get dropped.

science.title: New research compares civil servant experiences under Trump in the US to those under Bolsonaro in Brazil
science.summary: A new comparative survey of nearly 150 career civil servants (66 in the U.S. and 82 in Brazil) probed differences in bureaucratic responses to democratic backsliding among civil servants who served under U.S. President Trump and Brazilian President Bolsonaro.

science.title: A massive plume deep beneath Africa is pulling the continent apart
science.summary: A vast plume rising from deep inside Earth may be responsible for mysterious movements along the East African Rift. The discovery reveals how forces deep in the mantle are working alongside shallower geological forces as the continent slowly pulls apart.

science.title: NASA delays Crew-13 launch after leak found on SpaceX Dragon
science.summary: NASA and SpaceX have delayed Crew-13 after finding an oxidizer leak in the Dragon spacecraft’s propulsion system during prelaunch preparations. Engineers are investigating the problem before the four-person crew can begin its journey to the International Space Station.

science.title: AI searched 100 million possibilities and found a cheaper way to 3D-print a NASA rocket alloy
science.summary: Researchers used AI to search through more than 100 million possible settings for 3D-printing a high-performance NASA alloy. After only 40 experiments, the system identified six successful configurations, including one that worked at a record-low 500 watts. That could allow GRCop-42, currently difficult and expensive to print, to be made with much more widely available equipment.

science.title: “I jumped from my chair” – Astronomers spot Betelgeuse’s hidden companion
science.summary: Astronomers have captured their clearest image yet of Betelgeuse’s long-suspected companion, potentially ending a search that lasted about 100 years. The surprisingly massive hidden star could help explain Betelgeuse’s changing brightness and may influence its future supernova.

science.title: Your dislike of eating bugs may be 9,000 years old
science.summary: Ancient teeth and human DNA are revealing a surprising history of insect eating. Modern humans in northern Eurasia appear to have eaten insects only occasionally, while Neanderthals may have consumed them much more regularly. Populations near the tropics also retained genes that make insect exoskeletons easier to digest.

science.title: A mysterious cosmic hum may come from 13-billion-year-old dark stars
science.summary: Today’s mysterious gravitational-wave background may preserve clues about how the Universe’s first supermassive black holes formed. Descendants of hypothetical Dark Stars could be responsible for a major portion of the signal, offering a surprising new way to investigate cosmic dawn and dark matter.

science.title: Scientists switch on a strange new form of magnetism in an ultrathin material
science.summary: Scientists have found a surprising way to potentially switch on an unusual form of magnetism in ruthenium dioxide, a material that normally appears nonmagnetic. When the material was made into an ultrathin film only a few atomic layers thick and placed under strain, its electrons developed patterns consistent with altermagnetism, a recently proposed magnetic state with promising uses in advanced electronics.

science.title: 324-million-year-old fossil reveals how insects conquered land
science.summary: Ancient fossils suggest insects conquered land through a long amphibious phase rather than making an abrupt jump from water to dry ground. A newly identified 324-million-year-old species still carried paddle-like abdominal limbs, revealing an evolutionary bridge between aquatic ancestors and modern six-legged insects.

environment.summary: JANTHO, Indonesia — Illegal gold miners in Indonesia’s Aceh province have breached a crucial reintroduction forest for critically endangered Sumatran orangutans rescued from the illegal wildlife trade. “The result of our monitoring indicates that maybe dozens of excavators are suspected of operating in the Jantho forest area,” said Afifuddin, campaign and advocacy lead at the […]

environment.title: Superb fairywrens disappearing in Australia’s capital: Conserving insects could help save them
environment.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

environment.title: Recording a rainforest before Indonesia’s new capital changes it
environment.summary: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. In the forests around Pemaluan in East Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo, researchers led by Wendy Erb at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics in the U.S. have placed audio recorders on mountains, beside caves, and among […]

environment.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
environment.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: Imaging technique reveals the metabolic states of individual immune cells
mix_items.summary: When a patient is facing certain cancers or an immune condition, clinicians turn to white blood cells for clues about the progression of both diseases and their treatments. From a standard blood draw, a clinical lab isolates peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), which are predominantly immune cells, and then counts the abundance of different cell types, along with some basic measures of how they're functioning.

mix_items.summary: Rareș a învățat să creadă în propriile puteri datorită sprijinului educațional și emoțional oferit de Fundația Inocenți. Descoperă povestea lui. The post Rareș, băiatul care a învățat să creadă în propriile puteri appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.summary: The first thing that struck us wasn't the missing trees, but the missing water. In May 2026, we visited the Sundarbans, a mangrove forest in the delta where the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers meet in the Bay of Bengal.

mix_items.title: Protein buildup may shape cancer drug response
mix_items.summary: The way cancer-causing proteins accumulate in tumors may influence how effectively a promising new generation of medicines can remove them, a study suggests. Researchers found that PROTAC (Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras) drugs were more effective at removing proteins that build up because they are not broken down properly than proteins that cancer cells continually produce in large amounts.

mix_items.title: Q&A: Can you trust online ratings in the age of 'review bombing'?
mix_items.summary: Before buying a product, booking a hotel or streaming a movie, many people check online reviews. But not every glowing recommendation or one-star takedown reflects a genuine customer experience.

mix_items.title: Four-country study brings digital health coaching into everyday maternity care
mix_items.summary: Researchers at University College Dublin (UCD) have published the full study protocol for Bump2Baby & Me+ (B2B&Me+) in the journal PLOS One. The study tests how a digital health coaching program for pregnant women at risk of gestational diabetes performs when it moves out of a clinical trial and into routine hospital care. The publication coincides with the close of the study's recruitment phase, which began in December 2025 across hospitals in Ireland, Spain, Poland and Norway.

mix_items.title: Low-dose THC keeps breast cancer cells in tumor models from reverting to an aggressive state
mix_items.summary: Recent discoveries have revealed that breast cancer cells are more flexible than previously thought. Some can change from a differentiated state, when a mature cell has taken on a specific function, back to a more stem-like state. From there, they can become more invasive and resistant to treatment.

mix_items.title: Resin-mounted wallaby teeth reveal rare 1,200-year-old ornaments in Queensland
mix_items.summary: While sorting through animal bones in a rock shelter in Queensland, Australia, archaeologists came across a tooth where something was "not quite right." Stuck to the tip of its root was a blackish-brown ball of glue-like resin. Eleven more teeth with the same sticky substance were found, making them the only known instance of this type of tooth ornament found outside burials in northeastern Australia and the first in the Cape York Peninsula (CYP), the new study published in Australian Archaeology reports.

mix_items.title: Three common study myths busted by a learning expert—and better strategies to use instead
mix_items.summary: As high school and university students approach exam periods, study sessions often increase in frequency and intensity.

mix_items.title: Stress and depression, not heart damage, may drive long-term breast cancer fatigue
mix_items.summary: For breast cancer survivors, new research shows that feelings of depression and perceptions of psychological stress make the biggest difference in whether they experience fatigue up to two years after chemotherapy started.

mix_items.title: Children with speech sound disorders often face additional challenges
mix_items.summary: Speech sound disorders (SSD) in children are a common group of developmental difficulties that affect how speech sounds are planned and produced. In her thesis, "Oral Motor, Sensory and Developmental Indicators in Children with Speech Sound Disorders: A Clinical Cohort Study," Helena Björelius studied children ages 4 to 9 who had been referred for specialist assessment of speech and oral motor difficulties. The aim was to increase understanding of factors beyond speech itself, including chewing efficiency, sensory processing and medical and developmental risk factors.

mix_items.title: Severe asthma remains active in most despite widespread biologic treatment
mix_items.summary: Severe asthma affects around 5%–10% of all people with asthma and can involve recurrent exacerbations, impaired lung function and the need for corticosteroid treatment. In recent years, biologic therapies have improved treatment options for many patients.

mix_items.title: Investment in blood cancer research has saved nearly 26 million years of life, but disparities remain
mix_items.summary: Over the past 75 years, advances in the treatment of major blood cancers have saved more than 25 million years of life in the United States, according to results of an analysis led by researchers at Blood Cancer United and published in Blood Advances. But the gains have not reached everyone equally: survival progress remains limited for people diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and for Black individuals across most major blood cancer types.

mix_items.title: Old-growth tropical forests bear lasting legacy of ancient Maya civilization
mix_items.summary: Rainforests in Central America that have remained largely untouched by modern human activities could bear the invisible imprint of ancient Maya civilizations. New research has found that forest structure in Belize, such as canopy height and leaf density, may be influenced by how the Maya transformed and used the land thousands of years ago.

mix_items.title: Fieldwork safety emerges as a structural challenge for ecological research
mix_items.summary: A new Viewpoint in the journal BioScience argues that gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV) in ecological fieldwork should be understood not as a series of isolated incidents but as a structural problem rooted in how field research is organized, with broad consequences for the knowledge such research produces.

mix_items.title: Three distinct BMI trajectories identified in people with type 2 diabetes
mix_items.summary: A study by the University of Eastern Finland identified three distinct body mass index (BMI) trajectories among people with type 2 diabetes. Over the 10-year follow-up period, the BMI trajectories were associated with significant differences in comorbidities, diabetes medication and health care service use.

mix_items.title: Primary school food provision 'complex, fragmented and lacking central oversight', study reveals
mix_items.summary: A lack of central oversight and shifting catering models in primary schools could be putting children's dietary health at risk, according to new research led by the University of York.

mix_items.title: Major study reveals key differences in bowel cancer before and after age 50
mix_items.summary: One of Australia's largest real-world studies of younger adults with advanced bowel cancer has identified important differences between cancers diagnosed before and after age 50, which could help doctors tailor treatments for younger adults more effectively.

mix_items.title: Some of Australia's biggest companies are planning for an unbearable climate future
mix_items.summary: Even as unprecedented fires and heat waves rage across Europe, scientists track the retreat of Antarctic sea ice and a supercharged El Niño system heads our way, Australia's largest companies are forecasting business as usual in a much hotter world.

mix_items.title: Growing bacteria line up single-file, then buckle in liquid crystals
mix_items.summary: When scientists study bacteria that are not in a Petri dish or a test tube but in environments that more closely mimic their actual microbial habitats, they often find delightfully unexpected behaviors. For Sujit Datta, a professor of chemical engineering, bioengineering and biophysics at Caltech, those oddities are an invitation to apply physics to exciting new puzzles.

mix_items.title: Supplement plus chemotherapy boosts pancreatic cancer survival
mix_items.summary: When added to standard chemotherapy, a clinical version of the dietary supplement L-glutamine improved survival in an early-phase trial of patients with advanced pancreatic cancer. The study, led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University investigators, was published in Nature Cancer.

mix_items.title: Drone laser scans map more than 1,000 trees across 90-acre campus
mix_items.summary: It took one drone, 300 million laser data points and seven teams of students on foot to map Wake Forest University's trees. Led by Ovidiu Csillik, an assistant professor of remote sensing in the environment and sustainability studies program, the project produced a publicly accessible, interactive 3D digital map of more than 1,000 trees and helped the university earn international accreditation as a Level II arboretum.

mix_items.title: Men with low or high testosterone may have a higher risk of irregular heartbeat, review indicates
mix_items.summary: Men with either low or high testosterone levels may face a higher risk of atrial fibrillation, highlighting the need for personalized testosterone treatment, according to a review of existing evidence on testosterone and heart health published in the Journal of the Endocrine Society.

mix_items.title: Bees see the world in more ways than previously thought
mix_items.summary: The honey bee has held a special place in vision research. It is one of the best-studied insects, and much of what scientists know about how bees perceive the world is based on studies of honey bees.

mix_items.title: How breakfast primes the response to the hormones that manage blood sugar
mix_items.summary: Vanderbilt researchers have discovered why the adage, "breakfast is the most important meal of the day," holds weight—especially for the 1 in 9 adults worldwide living with diabetes. Glucose (the simplest form of sugar) is the body's main source of energy. When everything is working properly, the body regulates glucose—keeping it from spiking or crashing—and stores it until we need it.

mix_items.title: Mindfulness may lower blood pressure in just 8 weeks
mix_items.summary: Mindfulness, gratitude, and optimism training may improve blood pressure, inflammation, and other heart-health measures within just eight to 12 weeks. The strongest programs paired daily practice with regular reinforcement, suggesting that improving psychological well-being could become another tool for protecting cardiovascular health.

mix_items.title: London’s Ulez linked to healthier lung growth in children
mix_items.summary: Seven years after London introduced its Ultra Low Emission Zone, researchers are measuring the impact on children's health The post London’s Ulez linked to healthier lung growth in children appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: Three discoveries that transformed how we understand nutrition
mix_items.summary: When we think about nutrition, we almost always picture the same key players: the mouth, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas and perhaps the gut microbiota. However, the human body is not made up of isolated compartments.

mix_items.title: A supermassive black hole erupted in X-rays, and its radio jets followed 300 days later
mix_items.summary: By combining roughly two decades of observations from NASA's Swift X-ray Telescope with radio monitoring, astronomers have caught a supermassive black hole at the heart of the Perseus Cluster suddenly flaring in X-rays, and about 300 days later, its powerful radio emission flared too. Their paper describing the connection between this black hole's accretion disk and the jets it launches was submitted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 13 and accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Letters.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover why snake embryos twist into spirals
mix_items.summary: Snake embryos begin life curled into a distinctive right-handed spiral, and scientists may finally know why. Their bodies grow faster than their guts, creating a tether that forces the lengthening embryo to buckle and twist inside the egg. Researchers reached the conclusion after studying more than 900 embryos and using CT scans to reveal the hidden anatomy behind the coils.

mix_items.title: Reaching 90 without dementia doesn’t mean you’re in the clear
mix_items.summary: A study of people over 90 found that dementia risk remains strongly shaped by sex, race and genetics, with women and black participants facing notably higher risks. Intriguingly, some people stayed cognitively healthy despite carrying major risk factors, potentially offering clues to how the brain can resist dementia deep into old age.

mix_items.title: When exposed to air, new nanomaterial becomes magnetic at high temperatures
mix_items.summary: While fridge magnets are great for saving favorite recipes, modern magnetic materials are useful for improving fiber optics or quantum information science technology. On most fridge magnets the atoms are arranged in a repeated lattice structure called a "spinel." These structures are made up of three types of atoms, generically referred to as atoms "A," "B" and "X."

mix_items.title: The ethical use of AI in medical practice
mix_items.summary: A new ethics paper from the American College of Physicians (ACP) says that while the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical practice can improve health care efficiency and quality, it must be grounded in clinical integrity and professionalism. The paper, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, outlines three guideposts for the ethical use of AI in medical practice: rationality, self-governance and competence.

mix_items.title: GLP-1 RAs produce significant weight loss in adults without diabetes, with newer treatments showing greater results
mix_items.summary: An updated systematic review evaluating the efficacy and safety of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and coagonists among adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes found that, among currently available treatments, tirzepatide produced the greatest weight loss, while newer experimental drugs showed even larger effects.

mix_items.title: How do you get middle schoolers to eat more fruit? Give them smoothies
mix_items.summary: At lunchtime in rural Maine middle schools, University of Maine researchers stood at two points in the cafeteria.

mix_items.title: Engagement-driven curation can trap culture consumers in 'overfamiliarity,' leading to less long-term satisfaction
mix_items.summary: Sometimes you can be too good at your job. Take streaming services, like Spotify or Netflix. With engagement as their main goal, their recommendation algorithms typically identify the content a user engaged with most in the recent past and efficiently suggest more of the same. Content and genres that received limited engagement over a few weeks or months typically get dropped.

mix_items.title: What to know about dementia—and ways to prevent it
mix_items.summary: Dementia touches many lives—in many different ways. Most people have some firsthand experience of it, whether with an aging family member, friend or neighbor. More than 6 million people in the U.S. have some type of dementia, and that number is expected to increase in the coming years as the population gets older.

mix_items.title: New research compares civil servant experiences under Trump in the US to those under Bolsonaro in Brazil
mix_items.summary: A new comparative survey of nearly 150 career civil servants (66 in the U.S. and 82 in Brazil) probed differences in bureaucratic responses to democratic backsliding among civil servants who served under U.S. President Trump and Brazilian President Bolsonaro.

mix_items.title: The protein gap: Researchers highlight the importance of protein during menopause
mix_items.summary: New analysis from CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, has identified a protein gap among women ages 40–55, with survey data showing weight gain is commonly reported by women during the typical menopausal transition.

mix_items.title: Stay sharp after menopause: How aerobic exercise can improve key thinking skills
mix_items.summary: Regular aerobic exercise—the kind that gets your heart pumping—can improve important thinking skills called executive functions, and the benefits appear especially strong for women after menopause, according to Rutgers researchers.

mix_items.title: A massive plume deep beneath Africa is pulling the continent apart
mix_items.summary: A vast plume rising from deep inside Earth may be responsible for mysterious movements along the East African Rift. The discovery reveals how forces deep in the mantle are working alongside shallower geological forces as the continent slowly pulls apart.

mix_items.title: NASA delays Crew-13 launch after leak found on SpaceX Dragon
mix_items.summary: NASA and SpaceX have delayed Crew-13 after finding an oxidizer leak in the Dragon spacecraft’s propulsion system during prelaunch preparations. Engineers are investigating the problem before the four-person crew can begin its journey to the International Space Station.

mix_items.title: Goodbye CPAP? New sleep apnea pill cuts breathing events by 44%
mix_items.summary: A once-nightly pill cut breathing interruptions by about 44% in a major phase 3 sleep apnea trial, while improving oxygen levels and disease severity. By strengthening the muscles that keep the airway open during sleep, AD109 could offer a new option for people unable to tolerate CPAP.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a human-only gene that may help explain our brainpower
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered that human microglia, immune cells that help shape developing brain circuits, can take four to eight years to mature instead of just weeks as they do in mice. The unusually slow process may help explain how the human brain develops its remarkable complexity and cognitive abilities.

mix_items.title: High blood sugar may help cancer cells hide from the immune system
mix_items.summary: Researchers discovered a possible way cancer cells hide from the immune system: they build a thick, sugar-rich coating around themselves. High blood sugar can strengthen this protective shield under conditions that resemble the environment inside tumors, with the protein HSF1 playing a key role. Blocking this process could make cancer cells easier for the immune system to recognize and destroy.

mix_items.summary: JANTHO, Indonesia — Illegal gold miners in Indonesia’s Aceh province have breached a crucial reintroduction forest for critically endangered Sumatran orangutans rescued from the illegal wildlife trade. “The result of our monitoring indicates that maybe dozens of excavators are suspected of operating in the Jantho forest area,” said Afifuddin, campaign and advocacy lead at the […]

mix_items.title: Superb fairywrens disappearing in Australia’s capital: Conserving insects could help save them
mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

mix_items.summary: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. In the forests around Pemaluan in East Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo, researchers led by Wendy Erb at the Cornell K. mix_items.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
mix_items.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

mix_items.title: AI searched 100 million possibilities and found a cheaper way to 3D-print a NASA rocket alloy
mix_items.summary: Researchers used AI to search through more than 100 million possible settings for 3D-printing a high-performance NASA alloy. After only 40 experiments, the system identified six successful configurations, including one that worked at a record-low 500 watts. That could allow GRCop-42, currently difficult and expensive to print, to be made with much more widely available equipment.

mix_items.title: “I jumped from my chair” – Astronomers spot Betelgeuse’s hidden companion
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have captured their clearest image yet of Betelgeuse’s long-suspected companion, potentially ending a search that lasted about 100 years. The surprisingly massive hidden star could help explain Betelgeuse’s changing brightness and may influence its future supernova.

mix_items.title: Your dislike of eating bugs may be 9,000 years old
mix_items.summary: Ancient teeth and human DNA are revealing a surprising history of insect eating. Modern humans in northern Eurasia appear to have eaten insects only occasionally, while Neanderthals may have consumed them much more regularly. Populations near the tropics also retained genes that make insect exoskeletons easier to digest.

mix_items.title: A mysterious cosmic hum may come from 13-billion-year-old dark stars
mix_items.summary: Today’s mysterious gravitational-wave background may preserve clues about how the Universe’s first supermassive black holes formed. Descendants of hypothetical Dark Stars could be responsible for a major portion of the signal, offering a surprising new way to investigate cosmic dawn and dark matter.

mix_items.title: Scientists switch on a strange new form of magnetism in an ultrathin material
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found a surprising way to potentially switch on an unusual form of magnetism in ruthenium dioxide, a material that normally appears nonmagnetic. When the material was made into an ultrathin film only a few atomic layers thick and placed under strain, its electrons developed patterns consistent with altermagnetism, a recently proposed magnetic state with promising uses in advanced electronics.

mix_items.title: 324-million-year-old fossil reveals how insects conquered land
mix_items.summary: Ancient fossils suggest insects conquered land through a long amphibious phase rather than making an abrupt jump from water to dry ground. A newly identified 324-million-year-old species still carried paddle-like abdominal limbs, revealing an evolutionary bridge between aquatic ancestors and modern six-legged insects.

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.
